analysis.one_liner: Requires a federal license, safety training, and background checks to buy or own a firearm.
analysis.headline: Introduced December 17, 2025 with 7 Democratic cosponsors and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the same day; no hearing or vote has been scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for anyone to buy, receive, or keep a firearm without a federal license. To get one, a person would have to pass a firearms safety course with a written and a hands-on firing test, submit fingerprints and identification, and pass an expanded background investigation that lets state and local officials flag people who pose a danger to themselves or others. Each license covers a single firearm purchase and lasts five years. It would also close the private-sale loophole: any sale between people who are not licensed dealers would have to go through a licensed dealer for a background check, and private sellers would have to report their sales to the Attorney General within three business days. States with their own substantially similar licensing systems would be exempt.
analysis.who_benefits: People at risk of gun violence, since buyers would need safety training and a deeper background check than today's instant check, and private sales could no longer be done with no check at all. Police would also get a record of private transfers.

how_it_helps.text: It would be unlawful to purchase, receive, or possess a firearm without a valid federal firearm purchasing license, replacing the current system where most buyers need no license at all.
Applicants must complete firearms safety training including a written test on firearms law and hands-on firing testing, and submit to a background investigation, proof of identity, and fingerprints.

The Attorney General may deny a license to someone who poses a significant danger of bodily injury to self or others, based on factors like a history of violence, domestic violence restraining orders, stalking, or drug trafficking, and state and local officials can submit information supporting a denial; denied applicants can seek review in federal district court.
All private firearm transfers would have to go through a licensed dealer for a background check, closing the loophole that lets unlicensed sellers avoid checks today.

Anyone who sells a firearm would have to report the transaction, including seller and buyer identifying information and the gun's make, model, and serial number, to the Attorney General within three business days.
Licenses would be revocable, with notice, a hearing in district court within 30 days, and procedures to remove firearms from someone whose license is revoked.
States that already run their own licensing systems with substantially similar requirements could have their residents use the state license instead of the federal one.

analysis.who_pays: Prospective gun buyers, who would face training, fingerprinting, fees, and waits of up to 30 days per license per firearm; private sellers, who would have to route every sale through a licensed dealer and report it; and the firearms industry, which would likely sell fewer guns. Taxpayers would fund the new federal licensing system.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun buyers, private sellers, and the gun industry

drawbacks.text: Each license covers a single firearm and the purchase must happen within 30 days, so a buyer getting several guns would need several licenses, a much heavier burden than the one-time instant check system in place today.

The Attorney General could deny a license based on a broad list of factors judged 'significant danger,' including prior arrests without convictions and alcohol or drug abuse history, which gun rights groups would call an invitation to arbitrary denial, though denied applicants can go to federal court.

The bill creates a new federal licensing bureaucracy — background investigations, Rap Back enrollment, transaction reporting, and local offices in urban and rural areas — whose cost and staffing the bill does not specify.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safety case is real: universal background checks and a permit-to-purchase requirement are the policies most consistently linked in research to lower gun deaths. The cost side is also real: the single-firearm, 30-day license design is unusually restrictive even compared with state permit systems, and the discretionary denial standard depends heavily on how future attorneys general apply it. The bill asks a lot of law-abiding buyers in exchange for checks that most of the public tells pollsters it supports.

outcome.mechanism: It was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced, and nothing has happened since; the committee has not scheduled a hearing or a vote, and the full Senate has not considered it.

narrative.text: Senator Cory Booker introduced the Federal Firearm Licensing Act on December 17, 2025, joined by seven fellow Democrats: Senators Kim, Schatz, Warren, Blumenthal, Schiff, Padilla, and Hirono.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day, and the action history shows no further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote.

The bill text lays out a federal license requirement for acquiring or possessing firearms, a point-of-sale background check requirement for private transfers, and a reporting requirement for private sales.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has won yet, since nothing has happened; for now, gun sellers and owners are spared the new licensing and check requirements simply because the bill is sitting idle in committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun sellers and owners, for now

against.what_they_did: Has not brought the bill to the floor; no Republican senator cosponsors it.

sides.party_line_note: All eight senators behind the bill are Democrats, and no Republican has cosponsored it; with Republicans holding the Senate majority and the Judiciary chairmanship, the bill has stayed in committee.

industries.note: The licensing regime and per-firearm licenses would likely cut sales volume, but the bill hands dealers a guaranteed new role: every private sale must go through a licensed dealer for the background check, a service dealers can charge for. Dealers lose volume but gain a government-mandated gatekeeping position.

A license per single purchase, safety training, and expanded checks would shrink the customer funnel for new gun sales, costing manufacturers revenue. Ordinary people gain the safety rules that create that cost.

industries.industry: Private gun sellers and the resale market
industries.note: Unlicensed sellers could no longer complete a sale on their own; every transfer must pass through a licensed dealer and be reported to the Attorney General within three business days.

analysis.trajectory: With only Democratic support, a Republican Senate majority, and no committee action since referral, the bill is very unlikely to get a hearing or a vote in the 119th Congress; the realistic path is that it sits in the Judiciary Committee and expires when the Congress ends in January 2027, to be reintroduced only if control of the Senate changes.
